title: Critical Percolation as a Synthetic Data Model for Interpretability
abstract: Neural networks learn features that reflect the hierarchical, multi-scale structure of natural data. Synthetic datasets used to evaluate interpretability methods typically lack this structure, limiting their value as realistic toy models. To close this gap, we introduce a family of synthetic datasets consisting of hierarchical functions defined on critical mean-field percolation clusters embedded in a high-dimensional data space. The percolation data consists of sparse, low-dimensional fractal clusters with a power-law size distribution. Latent variables modeling a taxonomic hierarchy generate each data point's target value. The data model is analytically tractable with known critical exponents that fix its properties without requiring hyperparameter tuning. We leverage a mapping between percolation clusters, random trees, and additive coalescence to propose an almost linear-time algorithm to jointly sample a random tree and its hierarchical latent decomposition, enabling data generation at arbitrary scale. Using probing experiments, we find that the model's ground-truth latent variables can be linearly decoded from neural network activations. Together, sparsity, self-similarity, power-law statistics, and analytical tractability make critical percolation a principled testbed for interpretability research.
summary: This paper introduces critical percolation as a principled synthetic data model to test the limits of neural network interpretability. By generating data from sparse, self-similar fractal clusters whose structure is governed by random trees, the authors demonstrate that ground-truth hierarchical latent variables can be successfully decoded using linear probes on trained MLPs.
main_problem: Existing synthetic datasets for interpretability lack the complex, multi-scale structure found in natural data. The goal is to create a principled testbed that incorporates realistic structural features.
main_result: Critical percolation provides such a testbed because its inherent properties—sparsity, self-similarity, and power-law statistics—allow ground-truth latent variables to be linearly decoded from neural network activations.
method: The authors generate data by embedding nodes on critical mean-field percolation clusters, whose structure is mathematically mapped to random trees using an efficient cyclic coalescent algorithm. They then train MLPs and test linear decoding of the underlying hierarchical latent variables.
model_or_system: The model uses site percolation on a lattice approximated by the Bethe lattice in the critical regime ($p=p_c$). Data points are derived from sparse, low-dimensional fractal clusters whose target values are generated by a hierarchical latent variable decomposition based on the cluster's underlying random tree structure.
key_observables: Linear decoding performance ($	ext{R}^2$, MSE) of ground-truth latent variables; Cluster size distribution (power law $\propto s^{-5/2}$); Fractal dimension ($D < d$).
important_parameters: Critical probability $p_c$; Embedding dimension $d$; Latent variable depth; Figure of Merit ($	ext{FOM} \equiv s_{	ext{latent}} / \sqrt{s_{	ext{cluster}}}$).
main_assumptions: The model relies on the mean-field approximation ($d \gg u$) and assumes that targets follow a simple hierarchical construction. It also notes limitations regarding modeling compositional relationships.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the percolation data generation (fractal clusters, latent decomposition), validation of the cyclic coalescent process using Prüfer sequences and degree distributions, and probe performance comparing one-cluster vs. multi-cluster datasets.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the need for structured synthetic data. It then details the mathematical construction based on critical mean-field percolation clusters and their equivalence to random trees via coalescent processes. Finally, it applies this model by generating datasets (one/multi-cluster) and testing interpretability methods using linear probing of trained MLPs.
why_interesting: The rigorous connection between statistical physics concepts (critical phenomena, fractal geometry) and machine learning diagnostics provides a powerful, physically motivated benchmark for understanding feature representations in deep networks.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
